content: The diagnostic accuracy of the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (W4SS) for tuberculosis (TB) among people living with HIV varies depending on the population and the tools used. Programs may prioritize either higher sensitivity or higher specificity, and additional tools or combinations of tools can complement the W4SS to improve diagnostic outcomes. Evidence from six studies conducted in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda, involving 3,971 participants, showed an average TB prevalence of 14% (ranging from 1% to 26%). CRP testing with a threshold of >5 mg/L or >10 mg/L demonstrated similar or superior accuracy compared to the W4SS. The >5 mg/L threshold was recommended due to its higher sensitivity and its clinical relevance as the lowest threshold indicating abnormality. The choice of threshold depends on the available CRP technology, TB prevalence, and the need for either increased sensitivity or specificity. When CRP was combined with the W4SS in parallel screening, it achieved similar or higher sensitivity and specificity across populations, depending on the threshold and subpopulation assessed. However, among inpatients living with HIV, the specificity of CRP for TB screening was low, likely due to other comorbidities that also elevate CRP levels. Chest X-Ray (CXR) in TB Screening The WHO recommends using chest X-rays (CXR) in parallel with the W4SS to rule out TB disease before initiating TB preventive therapy (TPT) in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Data from eight studies across multiple countries, including Benin, Botswana, Brazil, and others, involving 6,238 participants, showed an average TB prevalence of 7% (ranging from 3% to 18%). CXR alone demonstrated similar sensitivity and similar or higher specificity compared to the W4SS across all subpopulations. When used sequentially after a positive W4SS screen, CXR had lower or similar sensitivity but higher or similar specificity. The choice of using CXR for any abnormality or abnormality suggestive of TB depends on the context, resources, and preference for sensitivity or specificity. Computer-Aided Detection (CAD) for CXR Interpretation In settings where trained personnel to interpret CXR images are unavailable, computer-aided detection (CAD) software offers a potential solution. CAD software was found to have accuracy comparable to human readers, with substantial overlap in performance. The WHO recommends CAD software that has undergone external validation and demonstrated non-inferior performance to those reviewed in 2020. However, limited data exist on CAD performance among people living with HIV, and further evidence is needed for better calibration in specific settings and populations. Molecular WHO-Recommended Rapid Diagnostic Tests (mWRDs) Molecular rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs), such as the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, are conditionally recommended for TB screening among adults and adolescents living with HIV in settings where TB prevalence exceeds 10%. A systematic review of 14 studies involving 9,209 participants showed no significant differences in accuracy between mWRDs and the W4SS followed by mWRDs. However, mWRDs are recommended as the initial diagnostic test for hospitalized patients living with HIV in high TB burden settings, regardless of symptoms, due to their high sensitivity and the critical need for rapid diagnosis in this population. In lower-prevalence settings, mWRD use alone may result in higher false positives and overtreatment. Lateral Flow Urine Lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) Assay The LF-LAM assay, a point-of-care test performed on urine samples, is recommended for diagnosing active TB in people living with HIV, particularly those with advanced HIV disease or serious illness. The Alere Determine TB LAM Ag is the only commercially available LF-LAM test endorsed by WHO. Evidence from 15 studies involving 6,814 participants (26% with TB) demonstrated improved sensitivity in individuals with low CD4 cell counts. LF-LAM is recommended as an add-on to clinical judgment and other tests, not as a replacement or triage test. Transition from Sputum Smear Microscopy to mWRDs Sputum smear microscopy, which has low sensitivity (approximately 50%) among people living with HIV, is being replaced by mWRDs as the initial diagnostic test for TB. mWRDs detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex bacteria and rifampicin resistance, offering higher sensitivity and accuracy. WHO recommends universal access to mWRDs for all individuals being evaluated for TB, including those living with HIV. Summary The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of rapid and accurate TB diagnosis among people living with HIV, given their atypical clinical presentations and higher risk of TB-related mortality. The use of CRP, CXR, CAD, mWRDs, and LF-LAM assays provides a range of diagnostic options tailored to different settings and populations. These tools, when used appropriately, can enhance TB detection and treatment outcomes in this vulnerable population.
